case_study_insert.main_stem: Tarn Polymer Works (TPW) is a private limited company in the polymer components sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2014 by Sofia Tarn, it moulds technical plastic parts for domestic appliance makers and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. TPW plans to invest $880,000 in a new injection-moulding press, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and produces 120,000 units a year. TPW faces a waste rate of 4.2% in moulding and a rising number of quality complaints from appliance assemblers in its Newton plant.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The press produced 30,000 parts in the quarter with a waste rate of 4.2%, up from 2.8% in Q2 2024. Customer complaints rose from 23 to 41 a month, and the batch rejection rate reached 2.6%. Delivery lead time averaged 4.4 days against a 3-day target. A survey of 500 appliance buyers found 57% would pay more for consistent quality and 35% had rejected a batch for visible defects. Retraining on the new press costs $650 per operator; 14 of 80 operators have completed it.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tarn Polymer Works as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (April 2026): (1) The central bank cut the base interest rate from 5.25% to 4.50%, reducing variable-rate loan costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $12.90 to $13.79 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale polymer resin prices have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while manufacturing inflation is 5.9% and domestic appliance sales are forecast to fall 1.5%.

questions.question_text: TPW is funding its $880,000 press with a $600,000 bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TPW of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or repayment, so TPW avoids increasing the fixed commitment on its $600,000 loan while it already carries $350,000 of fixed costs. The $280,000 saved in interest can be spent on retraining at $650 per operator, addressing the 4.2% waste rate and 41 monthly complaints, or on absorbing the 8.7% resin price rise without raising the $12.50 selling price.

Point 2: Internal finance keeps Sofia Tarn's control intact and avoids the security a lender would demand over the new press. A smaller loan also leaves TPW better placed if appliance sales fall by the forecast 1.5% and output drops below the 120,000 units needed to cover costs. Using $280,000 of profit demonstrates that the business generates enough cash to support part of the $880,000 investment, which could help if further finance is needed. Avoiding extra loan interest also leaves more of the $12.50 selling price available to meet the $650 retraining cost for the remaining 66 operators (80 − 14) who have not completed it.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TPW.

questions.question_text: TPW is trying to cut its 4.2% waste rate and 41 monthly complaints. Consider end-of-line inspection, quality circles, or a total quality management programme. Which should TPW choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
End-of-line inspection: Checking finished parts before dispatch is straightforward and would stop the 35% of buyers who rejected batches for visible defects from receiving faulty goods. It gives immediate feedback to the 80-strong workforce. However, inspection catches waste only after resin, machine time and labour have been used, so the 4.2% waste rate and the rise from 2.8% remain. With $350,000 fixed costs and a $600,000 loan, paying inspectors to sort scrap is less useful than preventing it, and the 4.4-day lead time against a 3-day target would lengthen.

Quality circles: Small groups of operators meet to find and fix the causes of moulding defects. This tackles waste at source, uses the knowledge of the operators, and suits a firm where only 14 of 80 have completed retraining. Circles can target the 41 complaints and 2.6% rejection rate directly, and they cost little beyond meeting time. Results depend on management acting on suggestions, and improvements may take weeks.

Total quality management: TQM embeds quality in every process and could transform the 4.2% waste rate and lift the 57% of buyers who would pay more for consistency. It is powerful but demands culture change, training across all 80 workers and sustained leadership — expensive and slow for a company servicing $600,000 of debt and a $880,000 press.

Recommendation: TPW should choose quality circles. They attack the causes of the 4.2% waste and 41 complaints at a cost the firm can afford while only 14 of 80 operators are trained. Inspection is rejected because it detects defects after the material is wasted, and TQM is rejected as too broad and slow given the loan burden. TPW can move toward TQM once circles have delivered results.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Names the three quality approaches with little reference to TPW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two approaches with applied reference to TPW's waste, complaints and training data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three approaches in TPW's context, recommends quality circles and explains why inspection and TQM are rejected.

questions.question_text: TPW's waste rate is 4.2% and only 14 of 80 operators are trained on the new press. Explain two benefits for TPW of on-the-job training for the remaining operators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: On-the-job training takes place at the press itself, so the 66 untrained operators learn on the machine settings that are causing the 4.2% waste rate. Learning is immediately relevant and can start cutting the 41 monthly complaints without the $650-per-person course fees, which would be expensive across a workforce of 80 while $350,000 of fixed costs must be met.

Point 2: Training on site keeps output of 120,000 units running, which matters because appliance buyers are forecast to fall 1.5% and TPW cannot afford lost capacity. It also lets the 14 already trained operators share experience under autocratic leadership, building consistency that supports the $12.50 price and the 57% of buyers who would pay more for reliable quality. Because the press makes 30,000 parts in a quarter, an operator who spots a moulding fault at once can stop a run before thousands of defective parts are produced for appliance makers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TPW.

questions.question_text: TPW must improve quality while its waste rate is 4.2%. Consider keeping its flat structure with autocratic leadership or moving to a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. Which should TPW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Flat structure with autocratic leadership: Few management layers keep decisions fast, and Sofia Tarn can act decisively to stop the line when the waste rate hits 4.2%. With only 14 of 80 operators trained, clear instructions from the top may prevent the inconsistency behind 41 complaints and a 2.6% rejection rate. The weaknesses are that operators closest to the moulding faults are not consulted, so their ideas are lost, and autocratic decisions can demotivate skilled staff, raising turnover when retraining costs $650 per person.

Hierarchical structure with democratic leadership: Extra layers give closer supervision of the 80 operators, while consultation lets operators suggest fixes for the 4.2% waste and 2.6% batch rejection. Involvement can raise commitment and reduce the 41 complaints because problems are reported upward quickly. Democratic decisions are slower, however, and more managers add to the $350,000 fixed costs at a time when the $600,000 loan must be served and appliance sales are forecast to fall 1.5%.

Decision: TPW should move to a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. The quality problem needs both closer supervision of an 80-worker plant and ideas from operators, which the present autocratic style suppresses. The flat autocratic option is rejected because speed alone has not stopped waste rising from 2.8% to 4.2% and complaints reaching 41. TPW should keep decision rights clear so democracy does not delay urgent line stops. With 30,000 parts made each quarter, a fault spotted by an operator can be escalated immediately through the hierarchy, whereas the present autocratic style relies on one manager noticing; that difference matters when 35% of buyers have already rejected batches.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two structures with limited application to TPW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Compares advantages and drawbacks of both options using TPW's waste, complaints and cost data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both options in context, recommends change and explains why the current flat autocratic structure is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TPW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $350,000 ÷ ($12.50 − $5.50) = $350,000 ÷ $7.00 = 50,000 units. | Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.50 − $5.50 = $7.00. | (iii) Four contextual uses explained.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $350,000 ÷ ($12.50 − $5.50) = $350,000 ÷ $7.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.50 − $5.50 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TPW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even of 50,000 units with 120,000 produced gives a margin of safety of 70,000 units, showing room to absorb the forecast 1.5% fall in appliance sales.
2. Contribution of $7.00 lets managers test price promotions: a $0.50 reduction from $12.50 leaves $6.50, so covering $350,000 needs 53,846 units.
3. Break-even of 50,000 units indicates the volume needed before the $600,000 loan can be repaid, guiding output targets for the $880,000 press.
4. Unit cost of $350,000 ÷ 120,000 + $5.50 = $8.42 benchmarks the effect of the 4.2% waste rate and helps decide if $650 retraining is worthwhile.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TPW's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TPW's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.28 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.44 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.88 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $150,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $295,000; 2025 current assets = $140,000 + $175,000 + $45,000 = $360,000. The broader liquidity measure is $295,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.28 in 2024 and $360,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.44 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($295,000 − $110,000) ÷ $230,000 = $185,000 ÷ $230,000 = 0.80 in 2024 and ($360,000 − $140,000) ÷ $250,000 = $220,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.88 in 2025.

Evaluation: TPW's liquidity has improved only modestly. The broader measure rose from 1.28 to 1.44, helped by current assets increasing $65,000 despite current liabilities rising from $230,000 to $250,000. However, the stricter measure improved from 0.80 to 0.88 and remains well below 1.0, so TPW still cannot cover short-term debts without using inventory. That is risky while it services a $600,000 loan and has committed $880,000 to a new press. Inventories grew to $140,000 even though the waste rate is 4.2% and 35% of buyers have rejected batches, so some stock may not be saleable. Receivables also rose to $175,000, tying up cash that could fund the $650 retraining.

Conclusion: TPW's liquidity has improved slightly but remains weak. The broader measure is better and cash rose to $45,000, yet the stricter measure at 0.88 shows continuing dependence on stock. Management should reduce inventories and collect receivables before drawing further on the loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated financial figures or vague comments about liquidity with no accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with some contextual comment on the trend for TPW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and current liabilities, and a justified conclusion on whether TPW's liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TPW of installing a computer stock-control system for its moulded parts.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Computer stock control tracks resin and finished parts in real time, reducing the 4.2% waste rate and the 41 monthly complaints caused by shortages or wrong batches. Better records help the 14 of 80 trained operators use material efficiently, protecting the $7.00 contribution per unit and the $880,000 investment in the press.

Disadvantage: Software, scanners and training add costs at a time when TPW already has $350,000 fixed costs and a $600,000 loan. With only 14 of 80 operators trained on the new press and retraining costing $650 per person, introducing another system could distract staff and slow the 4.4-day delivery lead time, which already misses a 3-day target. Real-time records would also identify which batches caused the 35% rejection rate, helping the 14 trained operators coach the others. The system must be introduced without disrupting output of 120,000 units, since a slower press would lengthen the 4.4-day lead time and add to the 41 monthly complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TPW.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate cut to 4.50%, the 6.9% minimum wage rise and the 8.7% rise in polymer resin prices will affect TPW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate cut (5.25% to 4.50%): The rate falls by 0.75 percentage points. If the $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the saving is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). This helps against $350,000 fixed costs but is small beside an $880,000 press, and if the loan is fixed the benefit arrives only on refinancing. Lower rates may also soften the forecast 1.5% fall in appliance sales.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, from $12.90 to $13.79): Each hour rises by $13.79 − $12.90 = $0.89. TPW has a workforce of 80 but the insert gives no hours worked, so an annual total cannot be invented. Productivity is 120,000 units ÷ 80 = 1,500 units per worker; if maintained, the $12.50 price absorbs the rise. With only 14 of 80 operators trained and $650 retraining costs, any fall in productivity would raise unit cost sharply while the waste rate is 4.2%.

Polymer resin inflation (8.7%): The insert does not split the $5.50 variable cost, so the defensible figure is an explicit bound: if all of it were resin-linked, 8.7% × $5.50 = $0.4785, about $0.48 a unit; at 120,000 units that is roughly $57,420 a year. Even a tenth, about $5,742, exceeds the interest saving and cuts the $7.00 contribution on every part.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in resin prices will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 120,000 parts, cannot be offset by a possibly fixed-rate loan and directly erodes the contribution funding the $880,000 press. The interest cut is helpful but conditional; the wage rise is bearable while productivity stays near 1,500 units per worker.
